On November 29, 1947, the UN voted to split one piece of land into two states. One side said yes. One side said no. Neither state on that map exists today in the shape it was drawn.

a thread 🧭🗺️

1/ Resolution 181 split British Mandate Palestine three ways: an Arab state (about 43% of the land), a Jewish state (about 56%), and an international zone around Jerusalem (under 1%) meant to stay separate from both.

2/ The Jewish share looked generous on paper. But Jews were roughly a third of the Mandate's population and owned a small fraction of the land by British survey figures — exactly what Arab leaders pointed to in rejecting the split.

3/ The Jewish Agency accepted the plan, reluctantly. David Ben-Gurion later said the borders weren't final, just a starting point. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected it outright and walked out after the vote.

4/ The plan was never carried out. Civil war broke out in Palestine within months. When Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, neighbouring Arab states invaded the next day, and the war redrew the map again — by force, not by vote.

5/ The 'international zone' for Jerusalem never happened either. By the war's end the city was split between Israeli and Jordanian control, not international administration — one more piece of the 1947 map that stayed on paper only.

6/ Almost 80 years later the 1947 lines are nobody's border, but they're still the reference point every later peace plan gets measured against — not where the lines ended up, but where the argument started.
